annotations.text:
CLEANER — every hard offset shadow gone, the ground flattened to a near-solid, and the press-down transform dropped. The 2px borders stay: they were doing the structural work, the shadows were only doing noise.

One consequence worth seeing before you decide. With the shadow gone, selection has nothing left to signal with but fill — so unselected options step back to a hairline border and 500 weight, and selected keeps the firm 2px rule and 700. The hue coding is carrying more than it used to.

Same layout, same palette, same sizes in both. Only the typeface differs.

EPILOGUE — the one you said felt most functional.

Holds up under the cleanup: the sharper terminals and slightly narrower forms give the rows definition that the flat treatment otherwise takes away.

And it stays recognisably yours.

INTER — as asked.

Genuinely excellent at UI sizes; that is why it is everywhere. Which is also the catch: it is the default UI face of a very large amount of software, so it reads as neutral to the point of anonymous.

Paired with a flat treatment there is not much left that is specifically Wino. Worth deciding on purpose rather than by default.

TEN FACES — each at the size it would actually run at.

All ten are on Google Fonts, which is the only font host the artifact can reach, and all ten carry the 600-800 weights this design leans on. Tap one to mark it.

Seven sans, two slabs, one screen serif. My picks are called out in the reply.

VINE, SETTLED. Type is the open question.

The accordion scale went up in all three: row labels 13px to 15px, values 16px to 18px, options 16px to 17px, rows 52px to 54px. That is the "bigger" change, independent of which face wins — it reads at arm's length on a table now rather than at reading distance.

All three are the same layout and the same palette. Only the typeface differs.

BRICOLAGE GROTESQUE — what you have been looking at.

Variable, slightly irregular, the most characterful of the three. The tight letterspacing on the bottle name is doing a lot of the playful work.

Tradeoff: the irregularity that makes it fun also makes it the least quiet at 15px, row after row.

GABARITO — rounder, more open.

Wider apertures and a taller x-height, so it holds up better in a dim room and at a glance. Friendly without being a toy face. Heavier top weight, so the bottle name still lands.

Tradeoff: more conventional. You lose some of the oddness that made Toybox feel like Toybox.

ZILLA SLAB — slab serif throughout.

The serifs add the seriousness you asked for two rounds ago without touching the colour, and slabs suit wine lists. Row weight drops to 600 because the serifs already carry weight.

Tradeoff: the most opinionated. Either it reads as confident or it reads as a coffee shop menu.

MY CELLAR — retrieve and review.

Search across grape, region and your own words. Filter chips for favourites and grape. Each bottle carries a coloured spine — same hue family as the axis chips — so the shelf is scannable by grape before you read a word.

Cards show the score, the star, and your takeaway, because the takeaway is the bit worth re-reading. Tapping one opens that session's explanation.

Shown in Bricolage; it inherits whichever face wins.

GROUND COLOUR — settled on Vine. Kept as the record.

The last artboard is the free-entry step that score and takeaway moved into.
THE ORIGINAL FOUR — kept as the record of the decision. Toybox was picked from these.
